title: Elihu: God Teaches Through Affliction
summary: Elihu begins his last speech by claiming to speak on God's behalf. God is mighty but despises no one; he watches the righteous, and when people are bound in affliction he shows them their sin and calls them to turn back. Those who listen are restored, and those who refuse perish. Elihu warns Job not to be drawn aside by bitterness, then turns to praise: God is great beyond our knowledge, the teacher without equal, and the rain, clouds, thunder, and lightning display his power.
story: Chapters 36 and 37 form Elihu's fourth and final speech, the longest of the four. It gathers up his earlier themes, that God speaks through suffering (chapter 33) and that God is perfectly just (chapter 34), and then turns decisively toward God's greatness in creation. That turn matters for the shape of the book. The dialogue between Job and his friends has run its course, Job has rested his case (31:40), and the reader is waiting for God. By the end of this chapter Elihu is describing a gathering storm, and within two chapters the LORD will answer Job out of the whirlwind. Elihu's closing hymn works like an overture to God's own speeches.
historical:
The chapter reflects the setting of the whole book: a pastoral and agricultural society on the eastern edge of the Israelite world, in the patriarchal era of the story, with no reference to Israel's kings, temple, or law. Its picture of kings enthroned and of prisoners bound in chains (verses 7 and 8) draws on the political realities of the whole ancient Near East, where fortunes could rise and fall abruptly and captivity in war or for debt was common.

The weather imagery at the end is rooted in the climate of the eastern Mediterranean and its hinterland. Rain there falls mainly in autumn and winter, often in heavy storms, and the whole agricultural year depends on it. A failed rainy season meant hunger. When Elihu says that by the rain and storm God judges the nations and provides food in abundance (verse 31), he is naming the single most important natural fact of life in that region: the same storm that terrifies also feeds.
cultural:
Elihu's claim to get his knowledge from afar and to be perfect in knowledge (verses 3 and 4) sounds arrogant to modern ears, and some interpreters think the book intends it to. Others note that the same phrase is used of God in 37:16 and suggest Elihu means that his words are sound and wholehearted, not that he is all-knowing. In a culture where the young were expected to defer to the old, his heavy self-justification also reflects the pressure he felt in speaking at all.

Verse 14 speaks of the godless dying in their youth among the qedeshim, a word the BSB translates male shrine prostitutes. The word means consecrated ones and refers to men attached to pagan shrines. Scholars have long assumed they took part in ritual prostitution, but many now question whether sacred prostitution was as widespread as once thought, and some think the word refers more broadly to disreputable cult personnel. Either way, Elihu uses it as a picture of a degraded life and a shameful early death. In the storm description, the pavilion of God (verse 29) draws on the ancient image of the heavens as the tent or canopy of a divine king.
literary: The chapter falls into two halves. Verses 2 to 21 are argument and appeal: Elihu restates the doctrine of discipline, God rescuing the afflicted by means of their affliction, and then applies it pointedly to Job with warnings in verses 16 to 21. Verses 22 to 33 turn to hymn. Two exclamations of God's greatness (verses 22 and 26) introduce two panels, the first on God as incomparable teacher and the second on the rain cycle and the storm. The Hebrew of verses 16 to 20 is notoriously difficult, and translations vary widely; readers should hold any single rendering loosely. The shift from argument to praise is the chapter's most important movement, since it points the book toward the storm from which God will speak.

outline.t: Elihu asks for patience to speak for God
God watches the righteous and disciplines the proud
The godless resist, but God rescues the afflicted by their affliction
Warnings to Job not to turn aside
God's greatness in rain, cloud, and thunder

doctrines.note: Elihu's central claim is that God can use affliction to open human ears. He rescues the afflicted by their affliction. The rest of Scripture affirms that suffering can discipline and refine (Hebrews 12:5-11), though Job's story insists that this is not the only reason people suffer.

God draws up the water, distills the rain, spreads the clouds, and directs the lightning. The weather is not a set of independent forces or rival gods but the work of the one Creator, who uses it both to judge and to feed.
God is mighty but despises no one; he is great beyond our knowledge and his years are unsearchable. Elihu joins God's power to his care for the lowly and his eternity to his nearness as teacher.

words.note: Oni, affliction or misery. Verse 15 plays on the related word for the afflicted person: God rescues the afflicted by their affliction. The line compresses Elihu's whole view of suffering into a phrase: the very thing that binds a person can become the means of his rescue.

Moreh, which can mean teacher and also the early rain that begins the Israelite agricultural year. In verse 22 it means teacher: Who is a teacher like God? Some interpreters notice that Elihu moves straight from God the teacher to God the giver of rain, and suggest the double sense of the word is deliberate, though that can't be proven.

Musar, discipline, correction, or instruction, a key word in Proverbs. In verse 10 God opens people's ears to musar and calls them to turn from iniquity. The word joins teaching and correction: it is the discipline a wise father gives a son.

Qadesh, literally a consecrated one, used for men attached to pagan shrines and translated male shrine prostitutes in verse 14. The term shows how Elihu pictures the end of the godless: a wasted life spent in degrading service to false gods.

christ: Elihu's idea that God rescues the afflicted through affliction finds its deepest expression in the New Testament, though Elihu himself is not speaking of the Messiah. The letter to the Hebrews applies the language of discipline to believers, calling it the mark of sons whom God loves (Hebrews 12:5-11). More strikingly, it says that Jesus himself learned obedience from what he suffered (Hebrews 5:8), not because he needed correction for sin, but because he walked the path of suffering fully as a human being. In Christ the principle is turned around: the innocent one is afflicted, and through his affliction the guilty are rescued. That is a thematic link, and the New Testament draws it with care.

hard.q: Does God send suffering to teach us a lesson?
hard.a:
Elihu says yes, at least sometimes: God binds people in cords of affliction to show them their pride and call them back. Many believers have found this true in their own lives, and Scripture supports it (Psalm 119:71, Hebrews 12:10-11). The danger is turning it into a universal explanation. Job's friends did that with punishment, and Elihu risks doing it with discipline, since he applies the doctrine directly to Job in verses 16 to 21.

The book as a whole resists that move. The reader knows from the prologue that Job's suffering was not caused by his pride and was not a lesson he needed; it was a test of whether faith can be real without reward. So the fairest answer is that suffering can become a means of God's teaching, and often does, but that we are not entitled to tell another sufferer what lesson God intends. Elihu's principle is true; his confidence about Job's case is the mistake.

questions: Elihu says God rescues the afflicted by their affliction. Has a hard season in your life opened your ears to something you would not otherwise have heard?
Why is it dangerous to explain someone else's suffering as a lesson God is teaching them, even if the principle is true?
Elihu turns from argument to praise at the sight of the storm. What happens to your questions about God when you stop to consider his greatness in creation?
